newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia looks set to slow tariff cuts.
newsitem.headline: Australia looks set to slow tariff cuts.

text.p: Australia, a leader in the free trade push among Asia-Pacific economies, will consider within days whether to slow its own programme of tariff cuts in the car industry in the face of high unemployment, industry anger and the end of broad political support for rapid reductions.
The Labor opposition on Tuesday joined unions and domestic car makers to urge the government to reject its main industry body's call for speedy and heavy cuts to car tariffs.

A community delegation from the car-making city of Geelong also travelled to Canberra to lobby against a Productivity Commission's recommendation in a draft report to reduce tariffs t0 five percent by 2004, from the current 22.5 percent.
Opposition leader Kim Beazley said a freeze was essential to foster business confidence and protect jobs.
"We have got to have a position which honours a decision by the major producers to invest here," he told reporters.
"There's something like 10,000 more jobs in the industry if we do the things that we said we should do."
Tariffs on imported cars are due to be cut to 15 percent by 2000. But the commission, a government advisory body, recommended continued reductions to bring rates down to five percent by 2004.
Critics say that will cost thousands of jobs, adding to the already high national unemployment rate of about 8.5 percent and carmakers warn the proposals would threaten their survival.
Four major carmakers have manufacturing plants in Australia -- Ford Motor Co, General Motors Corp, Toyota Motor Corp and Mitsubishi Motors Corp.
"We believe the Australian automotive manufacturing industry would not be here by the year 2010 (if the recommendations were adopted)," Mitsubishi spokesman Kevin Taylor told Reuters.

Prime Minister John Howard has said his response to the commission's final report, received last week, will be swift. He has opposed Labor's calls for a freeze, but signalled the pace will be slower than the commission recommended.
Howard said the government had to find a way to maintain a viable car industry and protect jobs, and meet its obligations to cut trade barriers under international agreements.
Analysts said the goverment is considering two options -- to gradually cut tariffs to 15 percent or 10 percent by 2005.

Labor's stand signals a dramatic turnaround for the leftist party, which in 13 years of government to 1996 waged an unprecedented campaign to axe trade barriers and open the once heavily protected domestic industries to competition.
But Labor's wideranging and deep tariff cuts sparked criticism that Australia was damaging its own interests by not insisting on matching benefits from other nations.
Australia is obliged to cut trade barriers by 2010 under the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) forum's ambitious free trade pact. Howard has reaffirmed his commitment to that target.
But the car tariff debate is seen as a test case for the pace and strategy used to reach the APEC goal.
Mitsubishi's Taylor said the industry did not oppose the APEC target if other countries also reduced tariffs and if Canberra maintained some export assistance.
South Australia state government leader John Olsen, a Howard ally, on Tuesday urged a slowing in tariff cuts.

"I'm calling on the Howard government to put investment and jobs in Australia ahead of any APEC commitments," he said, as the state parliament moved an urgency motion rejecting any tariff plan that would threaten the car industry.
